title: The innermost reliability zeros of complete graphs and Waldvogel's constant
shortTitle: How close the reliability zeros of complete graphs come to the origin
oneLine: The inner radius is set by a 1983 extremal constant for entire functions, and the zeros follow an explicit curve on 29/30 of the circle
abstract: The all-terminal reliability polynomial R_n(q) of the complete graph K_n gives the probability that K_n stays connected when each edge fails independently with probability q. Its complex zeros approach the unit circle as n grows. This candidate determines how closely they approach the origin: the smallest modulus h_n of a zero satisfies −n log h_n = 2 log n − 2(1 + log W_0) + o(1), where W_0 = 0.7377… is the rotation-restricted Whittaker constant studied by Waldvogel in 1983. Interval arithmetic shows that the innermost zeros approach the two directions arg q = ±2.393 (about ±137 degrees), not the negative real axis. On the arc π/30 ≤ arg q ≤ 59π/30, which asymptotically carries 29/30 of the zeros, a joint limit law for the angle and the rescaled distance to the circle holds with an explicit profile. For all sufficiently large n the negative real axis carries exactly one zero when n ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4) and none otherwise; exact computation confirms the count for 2 ≤ n ≤ 24. A short criterion based on the theorem of Hughes and Nikeghbali answers a question of Buys: the zeros of the spanning reliability of loopless matroids spread uniformly round the unit circle exactly when rank divided by size tends to zero. Limits: no explicit threshold for the negative-axis count; an arc of 1/30 of the circle near q = 1 is not covered; whether every zero lies inside the unit circle is open. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.
citeText: Anonymous (2026). The innermost reliability zeros of complete graphs and Waldvogel's constant. Version 0.1.0-candidate. Evidence Press. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24546697
evidence: A 15-page paper with a plain introduction, written proofs of every result, a section labelling every computation as exact, interval-certified or floating, the scope, open problems and an AI-use statement. Ten Python programs accompany it: exact counts of the real zeros for n up to 24, interval certificates (outward-rounded integer intervals, mpmath.iv and an independent Arb re-implementation) for Waldvogel's constant, the extremal directions and the 29/30 arc, a 120-digit finite-size comparison, derived constants and the figures. A clean replay in Python's optimised mode reproduced every recorded output; the arc program rejects two deliberately wrong inputs and a shifted enclosure makes the main certificate fail; Linux CI reruns them all.
statusDetail: Unrefereed AI-assisted mathematics candidate with written proofs and interval-arithmetic certificates for Theorems 9 and 10. Internal AI-assisted review: a combined five-perspective Claude review panel, one revision round, a re-review, a proof audit of the new and rewritten proofs, and clean replays with negative controls. No Astra/Codex review took place. External specialist review, independent reproduction and formal verification have not been established.
metadataProvenance: Prepared from the final paper (15 pages, with the release DOI), its programs and recorded results, the claim-to-output binding and the frozen release archive. The versioned GitHub and Zenodo research archives were checked against the frozen release assets on 26 November 2026.
keyResults: Theorem 8 (proof): −n log h_n − 2 log n → −2(1 + log W_0) = −1.39170…, so the innermost zeros sit at distance about (2 log n − 1.392)/n inside the unit circle; W_0 = 0.7377… is Waldvogel's rotation-restricted Whittaker constant.
Theorem 9 (computer-assisted): the innermost zeros approach the two directions ±2.393 radians (about ±137 degrees), not the negative real axis.
Theorem 10 (computer-assisted): on the arc π/30 to 59π/30, carrying 29/30 of the zeros, angle and rescaled distance obey a joint limit law with an explicit profile.

Theorem 7 (proof): for all sufficiently large n there is exactly one negative real zero when n ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4) and none otherwise, at distance about (2 log n − 1.517)/n from the circle; exact computation confirms the count up to n = 24. No explicit threshold.
Proposition 1 (proof): zeros of the spanning reliability of loopless matroids spread uniformly round the unit circle exactly when rank divided by size tends to zero, answering a question of Buys.

Credit and limits: Gilbert's formulas, Sokal's asymptotics for the deformed exponential, Waldvogel's constant, Hughes–Nikeghbali and Alsmeyer–Bostan–Raschel–Simon are classical inputs. An arc of 1/30 near q = 1 and a vanishing fraction of zeros are not covered; whether every zero lies inside the unit circle is open.
